messages.author: 2ffa956ce2411d70
messages.subject: WAIC for (joint) multinomial distribution
parts:
Hello everyone,

I am trying to implement WAIC for a simple case where the data comes from two multinomial distributions and am hoping to get feedback if my approach is correct. More precisely, WAIC requires the log-likelihood for each data point and sample, but with the inbuilt density function for the multinomial distribution we can only get the log likelihood for the whole multinomial distribution and not for the individual data points. Is it nevertheless appropriate to use WAIC in this case then?
For example, in my case I have two multinomials and then only get two log likelihoods per posterior sample.

A toy example follows below (using R and the loo package for WAIC).

Thanks,
Henrik

require(rstan)

d <- structure(list(db = c(200L, 1500L), bl = c(4460, 3860
), r = c(6002, 5350), npl = c(988, 905), c = c(11815,
12930)), .Names = c("db", "b", "r", "npl", "c"
), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")
d


m1 <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> n_200;
  int<lower=1> n_1500;
  int<lower=0> k_200[4];
  int<lower=0> k_1500[4];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> c;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> r;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> u;
}
transformed parameters {
  simplex[4] theta;
 
  theta[1] <- c;
  theta[2] <- (1 - c) * r;
  theta[3] <- (1 - c) * (1 - r) * u;
  theta[4] <- (1 - c) * (1 - r) * (1 - u);
}
model {
  // Data
  k_200 ~ multinomial(theta);
  k_1500 ~ multinomial(theta);
}
generated quantities {
  real log_lik[2];
 
  log_lik[1] <- multinomial_log(k_200, theta);
  log_lik[2] <- multinomial_log(k_1500, theta);
}

"

dat <- list(n_200 = sum(d[1,-1]), k_200 = unlist(d[1,c("c", "r", "b", "npl")]),
            n_1500 = sum(d[2,-1]), k_1500 = unlist(d[2,c("c", "r", "b", "npl")])  )

samples <- stan(model_code=m1,  
                 data=dat,
                 iter=1000
)

require(loo)
waic(extract_log_lik(samples))
## Computed from 2000 by 2 log-likelihood matrix
##
##           Estimate  SE
## elpd_waic   -145.9 1.0
## p_waic        69.5 0.7
## waic         291.8 2.1

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: WAIC for (joint) multinomial distribution
parts:
I didn't fully understand your model as the data is obfuscated by R code (I don't understand the lines which create d and dat).

The only parameters in your model are simplex[4] theta, so the maximum p is 3. Estimated p_waic is 69.5, so clearly you are doing something which does not work.

With the current code having two log_lik components and if you consider WAIC as an asymptotic approximation of leave-one-out cross-validation (which is ok, although it was originally derived as asymptotic approximation of genralisation error directly), then you can think whether you would consider it to be sensible to predict k_1500 given only k_200 and to predict k_200 given only k_1500? If this is sensible then you should do that exactly and not with WAIC approximation which works well only when you have much more observations than parameters. By "exactly" I really mean exactly, and not with PSIS-LOO in loo package. You can use the same code as for the k-fold-CV in our paper related to the loo package. If you would prefer leaving out only one observed value (not all for one multinomial as now), then it's more complicated, but even then WAIC is likely to fail since you don't have much data.

And finally: Why do you want to compute WAIC? What is your predictive task, which performance you are assessing?

Aki

parts:
Dear Aki,

Thanks a lot for your response. Unfortunately, I fear that I cannot follow your suggestion of directly using one of the data sets to predict the other one, as in my real model they receive different predictions (as shown below). 

My goal is to compare two or more different cognitive models that can generate predictions for the data and select the one that strikes the best balance between model fit and flexibility using WAIC, i.e., perform model selection (AIC could have be used for this task as well). The models usually have different numbers of parameters and can have quite different functional forms. The example model was a very stripped down version of one such model. In a more realistic case I would have also have a second version of that model that has one parameter or more to predict the difference between the two data sets (k_200 and k_1500; as can be seen from the proportion, there is a sizable difference in the proportion of c responses).

My ultimate goal is to do this in an hierarchical fashion. The current data is aggregated across a huge number of participants ( > 800) such that each participant contributes one multinomial distribution for each condition (k_200 and k_1500) with around 20 data points in each. So overall I have a lot of data. Nevertheless, before attempting the hierarchical version I wanted to know if and how I can actually use WAIC for multinomial data. How do I actually set up the log-likelihoods to get a reasonable value.

I extended my toy model to be more realistic and actually the estimate of p_waic seems more reasonable. I also added the output of the R code to show the data. I hope this works better for you.

Cheers,
Henrik

On Tuesday, December 8, 2015 at 1:57:10 AM UTC+2, Henrik Singmann wrote:
Thanks a lot for your response. Unfortunately, I fear that I cannot follow your suggestion of directly using one of the data sets to predict the other one, as in my real model they receive different predictions (as shown below).

If you can compute separate log_lik's as you have done now, then you can do what I suggested :)

WAIC is approximating pointwise predictive performance (or loss). What pointwise means is defined by how you divide the computation of log_lik in generated quantities. In your example here you have n=2 with respect to the asymptotic properties of WAIC. In our paper http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf we show that WAIC does not work so well if n is small (as in here).
My goal is to compare two or more different cognitive models that can generate predictions for the data and select the one that strikes the best balance between model fit and flexibility using WAIC
The best balance is the one giving best predictive performance, so you can just focus on that.

The models usually have different numbers of parameters and can have quite different functional forms. The example model was a very stripped down version of one such model. In a more realistic case I would have also have a second version of that model that has one parameter or more to predict the difference between the two data sets (k_200 and k_1500; as can be seen from the proportion, there is a sizable difference in the proportion of c responses).

It seems that this additional parameter is very useful. The previous results were likely to be really bad because the fitted parameter could not explain either k_200 or k_1500 and both parts were very influential. In the new model the new parameter helps but now it is likely that WAIC is slightly optimistic (due to reasons discussed in our paper), which may make the model comparison more difficult.

My ultimate goal is to do this in an hierarchical fashion. The current data is aggregated across a huge number of participants ( > 800) such that each participant contributes one multinomial distribution for each condition (k_200 and k_1500) with around 20 data points in each. So overall I have a lot of data. Nevertheless, before attempting the hierarchical version I wanted to know if and how I can actually use WAIC for multinomial data. How do I actually set up the log-likelihoods to get a reasonable value.

You can use WAIC (or even better PSIS-LOO) with multinomial data. And if the data is divisible so that you can compute more than two log_lik's in generated quantieties then things are better. Even then if you hierarchical model is such that each multinomial has it's own parameters and so that p_eff is large compared to n, then WAIC approximation is not accurate (see the above mentioned paper and http://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7461).

Additional benefit of PSIS-LOO is that it gives you khat values, which tells if PSIS-LOO or WAIC is likely to fail. It seems that we (i.e. Jonah) should add similar diagnostic directly to WAIC since people keep using it.
 
Btw. I once worked with multinomial model for cognitive data, but unfortunately we had lot of zeroes in the data and the results were extremely sensitive to prior. Luckily you seem to have much more data.

Aki

I extended my toy model to be more realistic and actually the estimate of p_waic seems more reasonable. I also added the output of the R code to show the data. I hope this works better for you.

Cheers,
Henrik

In your example here you have n=2 with respect to the asymptotic properties of WAIC. In our paper http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf we show that WAIC does not work so well if n is small (as in here).
 

My goal is to compare two or more different cognitive models that can generate predictions for the data and select the one that strikes the best balance between model fit and flexibility using WAIC

The best balance is the one giving best predictive performance, so you can just focus on that.
 
The models usually have different numbers of parameters and can have quite different functional forms. The example model was a very stripped down version of one such model. In a more realistic case I would have also have a second version of that model that has one parameter or more to predict the difference between the two data sets (k_200 and k_1500; as can be seen from the proportion, there is a sizable difference in the proportion of c responses).

It seems that this additional parameter is very useful. The previous results were likely to be really bad because the fitted parameter could not explain either k_200 or k_1500 and both parts were very influential. In the new model the new parameter helps but now it is likely that WAIC is slightly optimistic (due to reasons discussed in our paper), which may make the model comparison more difficult.
 

My ultimate goal is to do this in an hierarchical fashion. The current data is aggregated across a huge number of participants ( > 800) such that each participant contributes one multinomial distribution for each condition (k_200 and k_1500) with around 20 data points in each. So overall I have a lot of data. Nevertheless, before attempting the hierarchical version I wanted to know if and how I can actually use WAIC for multinomial data. How do I actually set up the log-likelihoods to get a reasonable value.

You can use WAIC (or even better PSIS-LOO) with multinomial data. And if the data is divisible so that you can compute more than two log_lik's in generated quantieties then things are better. Even then if you hierarchical model is such that each multinomial has it's own parameters and so that p_eff is large compared to n, then WAIC approximation is not accurate (see the above mentioned paper and http://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7461).

Additional benefit of PSIS-LOO is that it gives you khat values, which tells if PSIS-LOO or WAIC is likely to fail. It seems that we (i.e. Jonah) should add similar diagnostic directly to WAIC since people keep using it.
 
Btw. I once worked with multinomial model for cognitive data, but unfortunately we had lot of zeroes in the data and the results were extremely sensitive to prior. Luckily you seem to have much more data.

Aki

With the current code having two log_lik components and if you consider WAIC as an asymptotic approximation of leave-one-out cross-validation (which is ok, although it was originally derived as asymptotic approximation of genralisation error directly), then you can think whether you would consider it to be sensible to predict k_1500 given only k_200 and to predict k_200 given only k_1500? If this is sensible then you should do that exactly and not with WAIC approximation which works well only when you have much more observations than parameters. If you would prefer leaving out only one observed value (not all for one multinomial as now), then it's more complicated, but even then WAIC is likely to fail since you don't have much data.
